Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Despite acknowledgment from the White House a day earlier that a peace deal between Israel and the Palestinians is unlikely before a new U.S. president takes office, Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said Friday she is confident that ongoing efforts would produce success. Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni, right, and U.S.  Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice speak Thursday. "Carried to its state of conclusion, it will produce a state of Palestine," Rice, referring to negotiations in the wake of last year's U.S. summit on Israel-Palestinian peace in Annapolis, Maryland, said at a joint news conference with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas in Ramallah, West Bank. Rice is on her eighth trip to the region since the Annapolis summit. On Thursday, White House spokeswoman Dana Perino said the Bush administration does not "think that it's likely that it (a peace agreement) would happen before the end of the year." Rice said Friday that she realizes the lack of a peace agreement in the months following the Annapolis summit had caused some concerns that talks had stalled or might fail, but "it's quite the opposite -- the Annapolis process has laid the foundation for the eventual establishment for the state of Palestine." The purpose of her current trip, Rice said, was "to advance the Annapolis process," and while she did not speculate on a timetable for the future of the process or offer specifics on peace talks, she added, "I've seen them move forward a great deal in the past year." Both Israeli and Palestinian officials have expressed doubts about achieving a peace agreement before President Bush leaves office, but until this week U.S. officials had been more optimistic in their public comments. Speaking in Israel on Thursday, Rice blamed part of the inability to secure a deal on recent political changes in Israel, which she noted is "in the midst of elections." With Abbas on Friday, she emphasized that the commitment expressed by Abbas and Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert when they signed an agreement to work toward a peace deal by the end of 2008 is still strong. "I hope that the tremendous commitment (by both sides) is fully understood," Rice said. While Rice did not discuss any impact a new administration in Washington might have on the process, she said, "The United States really does understand why the Palestinian people want unity." Israel in recent months has seen political upheaval. Olmert resigned in September amid allegations of corruption. Kadima Party leader and Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni gave up efforts to form a new coalition government late last month and is seeking to hold early general elections, which could be held in February, Livni's spokesman has said. Olmert will continue to lead as Israel's interim prime minister until a successor assumes power either by forming a coalition in the current Knesset or through general elections. However, it is unclear whether he will be able to strike a deal with the Palestinians before Israel forms its new government. Last month, Rice postponed a trip to a Middle East conference because of the global crisis in financial markets.

She was referring to the talks that emerged from the previous year's American summit on peace between Israel and the Palestinians, held in Annapolis, Maryland.

This marked Rice's eighth journey to the region since that Annapolis gathering. The day before, White House spokeswoman Dana Perino stated that the Bush administration did not "think that it's likely that it [a peace agreement] would happen before the end of the year."

On Friday, Rice acknowledged her awareness that the absence of any peace accord in the months since Annapolis had raised worries that the negotiations had ground to a halt or could ultimately collapse. Yet she insisted the reality was "quite the opposite -- the Annapolis process has laid the foundation for the eventual establishment for the state of Palestine."

According to Rice, the objective of her latest visit was "to advance the Annapolis process." Though she declined to predict a schedule for how the process might unfold or to reveal particulars about the peace discussions, she remarked, "I've seen them move forward a great deal in the past year."

Officials on both the Israeli and Palestinian sides have voiced skepticism regarding the possibility of finalizing a peace deal before President Bush departs office. Until this week, however, American representatives had struck a more hopeful tone in their public statements.

During remarks in Israel on Thursday, Rice attributed part of the failure to reach an agreement to the recent political shifts within Israel, a nation she pointed out was "in the midst of elections." Standing beside Abbas on Friday, she stressed that the pledge made by both Abbas and Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert -- when they signed a deal committing to pursue peace by the close of 2008 -- remained firm. "I hope that the tremendous commitment [by both sides] is fully understood," Rice said.

Although Rice avoided addressing how an incoming Washington administration could affect the negotiations, she observed, "The United States really does understand why the Palestinian people want unity."

Israel has experienced considerable political turmoil over the past several months. Olmert stepped down in September while facing corruption accusations. Late last month, Kadima Party leader and Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni abandoned her attempt to assemble a new coalition government and is now pushing for early general elections, which her spokesman indicated could take place in February.

Olmert will remain in charge as Israel's caretaker prime minister until his replacement takes over, either by building a coalition within the existing Knesset or via general elections. It remains uncertain, though, whether he can reach an agreement with the Palestinians before Israel establishes its new government.

Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice expressed confidence that ongoing negotiations would ultimately succeed in producing an independent Palestinian state, offering a note of optimism even as questions mounted over the pace and prospects of the peace process.

Rice's statement came a day after White House spokeswoman Dana Perino acknowledged that a peace agreement was unlikely to be reached before the end of the Bush administration's term. The admission marked a notable shift in tone from the confident predictions that had characterized earlier stages of the diplomatic effort.

Nevertheless, Rice sought to reframe the significance of the negotiations. Rather than characterizing the process as stalled, she argued that the Annapolis process had successfully laid the foundation for the eventual establishment of a Palestinian state. In her view, the diplomatic groundwork accomplished during this period represented meaningful progress, even if a final agreement remained out of reach within the administration's timeframe.

Her comments came against a backdrop of growing skepticism from key parties to the negotiations. Both Israeli and Palestinian officials had expressed doubts about the likelihood of reaching a peace deal before President Bush left office—a sentiment that stood in sharp contrast to the earlier optimism voiced by U.S. officials when the talks began.

Addressing the reasons behind the failure to secure a final agreement, Rice attributed part of the difficulty to recent political changes in Israel, which was in the midst of elections. The resulting political uncertainty, she suggested, had complicated efforts to bring the negotiations to a definitive conclusion within the anticipated timeframe.

# Rice Expresses Continued Optimism on Israeli-Palestinian Peace Despite Diminished Expectations

Even as the White House openly conceded that a comprehensive Israeli-Palestinian peace agreement was improbable before President George W. Bush left office, Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice struck a notably optimistic tone during her latest diplomatic mission to the region. On this, her eighth trip since the Annapolis conference launched renewed peace negotiations, Rice expressed firm confidence that the ongoing talks between Israeli and Palestinian leaders would ultimately bear fruit, even if the timeline extended beyond the current administration.

The acknowledgment from Washington represented a candid assessment of the difficult realities facing the peace process. The ambitious goals set forth at Annapolis had proven more challenging to achieve than initially hoped, and the political calendar left little room for the kind of breakthrough that would produce a signed agreement in the administration's remaining months.

Nevertheless, Rice remained steadfast in her belief that the diplomatic groundwork was meaningful and durable. She maintained that the Annapolis process had successfully laid the essential foundation for eventually establishing an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel. In her view, the framework and momentum created through these negotiations would continue to serve as a basis for future progress, regardless of when a final deal might be reached.

Notably, Rice declined to offer any specific timetable for when such an agreement might be concluded. Instead, she pointed to several factors complicating the pace of negotiations, including the political uncertainty surrounding Israel's ongoing elections. The electoral transition in Israel had introduced a period of instability that made it difficult to advance the delicate discussions, as leadership questions and shifting political priorities inevitably affected the government's capacity to make significant concessions or commitments.

In attributing part of the stalled progress to these domestic Israeli political dynamics, Rice sought to frame the current impasse as a temporary obstacle rather than a fundamental failure of the peace initiative itself. Her message emphasized continuity and long-term commitment, suggesting that while the Bush administration might not witness the culmination of its diplomatic efforts, the process it had set in motion would endure and eventually succeed.

counterfactuals.output:
# Rice Presses for Progress on Palestinian Statehood During West Bank Visit

**RAMALLAH, West Bank (CNN)** — U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice met with Palestinian leaders in the West Bank on Wednesday, pledging continued American support for peace negotiations and urging both sides to build on the momentum generated by last month's Annapolis summit.

Speaking after talks with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas in Ramallah, Rice said the United States remained committed to the goal of establishing a Palestinian state and emphasized that the window of opportunity opened at Annapolis must not be squandered.

"The time has come for the establishment of a Palestinian state," Rice told reporters. "The United States is committed to working with both parties to achieve this goal, and we expect both sides to fulfill their obligations."

## Building on Annapolis

The November summit in Annapolis, Maryland, brought together Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert and Abbas, along with representatives from dozens of nations, in the most significant push for Middle East peace in years. The two leaders agreed to launch formal negotiations with the aim of reaching a peace agreement by the end of 2008.

Rice acknowledged that difficult challenges lie ahead but expressed optimism that a durable agreement was within reach.

"There will be tough issues to resolve," she said. "But I believe both leaders are serious about seizing this opportunity. The alternative — continued conflict and suffering — serves no one."

## Roadmap Obligations

Rice reiterated the importance of both parties meeting their commitments under the internationally backed "roadmap" peace plan. Palestinians are required to crack down on militant groups, while Israel is expected to freeze settlement construction and ease restrictions on Palestinian movement.

Abbas, speaking alongside Rice, called on Israel to halt settlement activity, which Palestinians view as a major obstacle to peace.

"Settlement expansion undermines the trust necessary for successful negotiations," Abbas said through a translator. "We look to our American partners to help ensure that commitments are honored."

## Challenges Remain

Rice's visit comes amid ongoing tensions, including continued violence in and around Gaza, which remains under the control of Hamas after the Islamist group seized the territory in June. The division between Hamas-controlled Gaza and the Abbas-led West Bank continues to complicate peace efforts.

Analysts note that core issues — including the status of Jerusalem, the fate of Palestinian refugees, final borders, and security arrangements — remain deeply contentious and have derailed previous negotiations.

Rice, who was scheduled to meet with Israeli officials later in her trip, said she would continue shuttling between the parties in the coming months to help sustain the negotiating process.

"This is going to require patience, hard work and courage from both sides," she said. "But the United States will remain engaged every step of the way."

Rice is expected to make several return visits to the region in the months ahead as negotiations move forward.

---

*This article is a dramatized recreation reflecting the general tone and content of news coverage from the post-Annapolis period in late 2007. Specific quotations are illustrative.*

**RAMALLAH, West Bank** — Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice appeared alongside Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas at a joint press conference here, where she addressed the ongoing efforts to broker a peace agreement between Israelis and Palestinians while acknowledging the significant challenges that remain.

Bush completes his term in office. Despite earlier hopes that the Annapolis process might yield a historic accord, officials have increasingly signaled that the ambitious goal may not be met on schedule.

The tempered expectations mark a notable shift from the optimism that surrounded the launch of renewed negotiations, when both sides expressed willingness to work toward resolving longstanding disputes.

## Abbas Reaffirms Palestinian Position

President Abbas, for his part, used the occasion to underscore Palestinian priorities in the negotiations, including core issues that have long complicated the path to a two-state solution.

## Looking Ahead

# Diplomatic Push for Palestinian Statehood Falters Amid Israeli Political Upheaval

*A retrospective news feature on the events of 2008*

## Annapolis Momentum Meets Domestic Instability

The diplomatic architecture erected at the November 2007 Annapolis Conference, which had raised hopes for a negotiated two-state solution by the end of 2008, entered the year under significant strain as Israel's domestic political situation grew increasingly precarious.

The conference, hosted by the outgoing Bush administration, had committed Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert and Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas to a framework of bilateral negotiations. Both leaders had publicly endorsed the goal of reaching a peace agreement before President George W. Bush left office in January 2009—an ambitious timeline that observers increasingly viewed as unrealistic.

## Olmert Under Legal and Political Siege

Prime Minister Olmert's authority eroded steadily throughout the spring and summer of 2008 as a series of corruption investigations gathered momentum. The most damaging allegations centered on claims that Olmert had improperly accepted cash-filled envelopes from American businessman Morris Talansky, whose testimony in May dealt a severe blow to the prime minister's standing.

As pressure mounted, Olmert announced on July 30 that he would not contest the leadership of his centrist Kadima party in upcoming primaries and would step down as prime minister once a successor was chosen. The announcement, while framed as a defense against what Olmert characterized as an unfair rush to judgment, effectively transformed him into a lame-duck leader during a critical phase of negotiations.

Despite his diminished position, Olmert continued to pursue talks with Abbas, reportedly floating far-reaching proposals on territorial withdrawal, Jerusalem, and refugee questions. However, his weakened political mandate raised serious doubts about whether any agreement he might reach could survive domestic ratification.

## Livni's Ascent and the Coalition Challenge

The Kadima leadership contest concluded on September 17, 2008, with Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni narrowly defeating Transportation Minister Shaul Mofaz. A former Mossad officer and lawyer, Livni had built a reputation as a pragmatic negotiator and had served as a lead Israeli representative in the Annapolis-track talks.

Her victory positioned her to become Israel's second female prime minister, following Golda Meir. President Shimon Peres formally tasked Livni with forming a new government, giving her the standard period to assemble a governing coalition within the fractured Knesset.

Livni's coalition-building efforts, however, quickly ran aground. Negotiations with the ultra-Orthodox Shas party proved particularly contentious, with Shas demanding substantial increases in family welfare subsidies and, critically, a commitment that Jerusalem's status would not be negotiated. Livni, unwilling to meet Shas's financial demands or to foreclose diplomatic flexibility on Jerusalem, refused to yield.

On October 26, 2008, Livni announced that she had been unable to form a viable coalition and called for early elections rather than accept what she described as untenable political blackmail. The decision, while praised by some as principled, meant that Israel would head to elections scheduled for February 2009, leaving Olmert as caretaker prime minister in the interim.

## Implications for the Peace Process

The collapse of Livni's coalition efforts dealt a decisive blow to the Annapolis timeline. With Israel entering an election campaign, meaningful negotiations were effectively frozen. Palestinian officials expressed frustration that the diplomatic window opened at Annapolis was closing without tangible results.

The situation on the Palestinian side compounded these difficulties. The territorial and political split between Abbas's Fatah-led Palestinian Authority in the West Bank and Hamas, which controlled the Gaza Strip following its 2007 takeover, meant that even a willing Israeli partner would have faced questions about whether Abbas could deliver on any comprehensive agreement.

Analysts noted several structural obstacles that persisted throughout the year:

- **Settlement expansion** in the West Bank continued, undermining Palestinian confidence in Israeli intentions
- **Core final-status issues**—borders, Jerusalem, refugees, and security arrangements—remained unresolved despite intensive discussions
- **Political weakness on both sides** left neither leader with the mandate necessary for historic compromises

## International Reaction

The international community, including the Middle East Quartet (the United States, Russia, the European Union, and the United Nations), continued to express rhetorical support for the two-state framework. Quartet envoy Tony Blair emphasized economic development and institution-building in the West Bank as complementary tracks to political negotiations.

The incoming American administration of President-elect Barack Obama, who won the November 2008 election, was expected to bring renewed attention to the conflict, though the specific contours of its approach remained uncertain as the year drew to a close.

## An Unfulfilled Year

By December 2008, the aspiration to achieve Palestinian statehood within the year had clearly gone unmet. The confluence of Olmert's legal troubles, the leadership transition within Kadima, and Livni's failure to secure a governing majority had consumed political energy that might otherwise have advanced negotiations.

The year concluded with tensions escalating dramatically as Israel launched a major military operation in Gaza in late December, further complicating the diplomatic landscape and underscoring how far the parties remained from the vision articulated at Annapolis just over a year earlier.

---

*This retrospective examines the diplomatic and political developments of 2008 based on the historical record of that period.*

# Optimism Meets Skepticism: The Widening Gap Over 2008 Peace Deadline

## U.S. Officials Project Confidence as Regional Actors Voice Doubts

A notable divide has emerged between Washington's public optimism about brokering a Middle East peace agreement by the end of 2008 and the more sober assessments coming from both Israeli and Palestinian officials on the ground.

### The American Position

Following the momentum generated by the Annapolis Conference, U.S. officials have repeatedly expressed confidence that a comprehensive peace agreement could be reached within the year. Administration officials have framed the timeline as ambitious but achievable, pointing to renewed negotiations and the personal commitment of senior American diplomats who have made frequent trips to the region.

The optimism reflects a strategic desire to secure a diplomatic legacy achievement and capitalize on what officials describe as a rare alignment of political will among the parties involved.

### Israeli Caution

Israeli officials, while participating in negotiations, have tempered expectations. Concerns center on several persistent obstacles:

- **Security guarantees** that many Israeli leaders consider prerequisites for any territorial concessions
- **The political fragmentation** of Palestinian leadership, particularly the division between the West Bank and Gaza
- **Domestic political constraints** that complicate the government's ability to make sweeping commitments

Some Israeli figures have suggested that while progress is possible, framing success around a specific calendar deadline risks setting up the process for perceived failure.

### Palestinian Reservations

Palestinian officials have expressed their own skepticism, citing:

- **Continued settlement activity** that they argue undermines the viability of negotiations
- **Movement and access restrictions** affecting daily life and economic conditions
- **Doubts about whether core issues**—including borders, refugees, and the status of Jerusalem—can be resolved in such a compressed timeframe

Palestinian leaders have also pointed to internal divisions that complicate their negotiating position and their capacity to implement any eventual agreement.

### The Core Tension

The divergence highlights a fundamental question: whether diplomatic optimism serves to build momentum or risks generating expectations that outpace realities on the ground. Analysts note that the core "final status" issues that have derailed previous negotiations remain largely unresolved, and that resolving them within months would require concessions that neither side appears prepared to make.

### Looking Ahead

As the deadline approaches, the gap between aspiration and expectation raises questions about the consequences of falling short. Whether the timeline proves to be a productive catalyst or an overly optimistic benchmark remains to be seen, but the differing assessments underscore the enduring complexity of one of the world's most intractable conflicts.

---

*Note: This article is written in a general journalistic style reflecting the diplomatic dynamics of the 2007–2008 Annapolis peace process period. For specific quotes, attributions, and current developments, readers should consult primary news sources from that time.*

# Rice Returns to Middle East, Voices Optimism Despite Deadlock

**JERUSALEM** — Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice arrived in the region Wednesday for her eighth diplomatic mission since the Annapolis conference, expressing continued confidence that Israeli and Palestinian negotiators can reach a peace agreement despite mounting evidence of stalled talks.

Rice, who has made shuttle diplomacy between Jerusalem and the West Bank a centerpiece of her final year in office, sought to project optimism even as negotiators on both sides acknowledged deep divisions over core issues.

"I have no doubt that there will be a Palestinian state," Rice told reporters shortly after landing. "The question is not whether, but when. The parties are committed to this process, and I remain confident that we can help them achieve their goals."

The Secretary's remarks came against a backdrop of skepticism among regional observers, who have questioned whether meaningful progress can be achieved before the current U.S. administration leaves office.

Negotiations launched at the November Annapolis conference set an ambitious goal of reaching a comprehensive peace deal by year's end. But talks have been repeatedly complicated by disputes over Israeli settlement construction, the status of Jerusalem, and security arrangements.

Palestinian officials have expressed frustration over continued settlement activity, which they say undermines the negotiations. Israeli leaders, meanwhile, have cited security concerns amid ongoing tensions.

Rice was scheduled to meet separately with Israeli Prime Minister and Palestinian Authority President during her visit, in an effort to bridge the gaps between the two sides.

"These are difficult issues that have defied resolution for decades," Rice acknowledged. "But I believe the leaders on both sides understand the historic opportunity before them."

The Secretary declined to offer specifics on the substance of the negotiations, citing the sensitivity of the ongoing discussions.

Critics have suggested that the frequency of Rice's visits reflects the difficulty of the diplomatic effort rather than its success. But administration officials maintain that sustained high-level engagement remains essential to keeping the peace process alive.

Rice is expected to remain in the region for several days of talks before returning to Washington.
